intro: You can already signpost a talk, explain a chart and answer questions honestly, and you know how to make your key words stand out with pitch and pauses. Now you'll make a presentation **persuasive**: open with a hook, tell a short story with a point, end with a clear call to action, speak from brief notes instead of a script, and stay calm when the questions get difficult. Warm-up: think of a talk that really convinced you. What do you still remember from it?
teachingNotes: This speaking lesson (strand SP) builds on its chain; recap each in a line, don't re-teach: b2-presentations (signposts: Today I'd like to talk about …; I've divided my talk into three parts; Let's move on to …; That brings me to …; To sum up, …; The key takeaway is that …; the four Q&A moves: welcome, check, answer briefly, check back with Does that answer your question?; I'm afraid = sayangnya; no opening apology; don't read the slide) and c1-pron-prosody (step up on the key word, fall ↘ at the end of a point, thought groups, a pause for effect before a key number, silence instead of 'eee…'). New here: storytelling to persuade (hooks, a four-part story, concrete detail, past tenses for the story and present for the point, the rule of three, a call to action), speaking from keyword notes, and handling difficult, hostile or off-topic questions. Contexts: a bank in Surabaya, a logistics startup in Jakarta, an NGO in Lombok, a clinic in Yogyakarta, a university seminar in Bandung, investors, ministries; Rina, Budi, Sari, Dimas, Pak Hasan, Bu Ani, Dr. Wulan. All figures and stories are practice examples.

Storytelling. A hook (pengait) is the first 20–30 seconds that make people want to listen: a question to the audience (How many of you …?), a surprising number (Last year, one in four of our new customers left within a month.) or a very short story (Last March, Bu Siti …). Name, role and topic can come right after the hook, briefly. A persuasive story has four parts: the situation (who, where, when), the turning point (the moment the problem became clear), the change (what was done and what happened), and the lesson for the audience (the point, linked to what you want them to do). Concrete detail makes it believable: a name, a place, a number (Pak Joko, a batik seller in Solo, lost three orders a week), not 'many customers have problems'. Tenses: past simple and past continuous for the story (called, was losing), present for the point (That's why I believe we need …). Native speakers sometimes tell informal stories in the present ('So last week this customer calls me …'): that's a style choice; don't mark it wrong in free speech, but recommend the past in a presentation and never mixing the two at random. Rule of three: three reasons or three benefits sound complete and are easy to remember (faster, cheaper and safer), with the voice falling ↘ on the last item. Call to action (ajakan bertindak) = who does what by when (So I'm asking you to approve a three-month pilot in Bandung, starting in January.).

Likely errors (the node lists none; these are the ones to watch): (1) an opening that is only 'Good morning, my name is …, today I will talk about …', or a long thank-you opening (Pertama-tama, puji syukur …; terima kasih kepada Bapak Direktur, Bapak/Ibu manajer, panitia …) that uses the best 30 seconds of the talk; (2) a story with no point, or no concrete detail ('Many customers have problems'); (3) missing past endings in the story ('Last month a customer call us' → called: Indonesian has no tense marking) or a point told in the past; (4) ending with 'That's all. Thank you.' or 'Okay, that's it' with no call to action; (5) writing the whole script on cards or slides and reading it, or memorising it word for word (hafalan), so one forgotten word stops everything; (6) losing your place and saying 'Sorry, sorry, I forgot … eee … apa ya' instead of a silent pause and 'Where was I? Right, …'; (7) in Q&A: interrupting the questioner, getting defensive ('That's not true. You don't understand.'), bluffing, a bare 'I don't know' or 'No comment', or ignoring an off-topic question.

Speaking from notes: keyword notes are 2–6 words per idea, mainly names, numbers and the key noun or verb (Surabaya delivery: 5 → 2 days (new warehouse)), never full sentences. Reading aloud sounds flat because the eyes are on the paper (no eye contact) and written sentences are long, so the voice loses its pitch range and natural pauses (recap c1-pron-prosody). Rehearsal: write a full draft once, cut it to keywords, say it aloud from the keywords three or four times (different words each time is fine), time it, record yourself or practise with a colleague; memorise only the first and last lines (the hook and the call to action). Slides as prompts: one idea per slide, a short headline plus a number or picture, so the slide reminds you what to say and the audience listens to you. Recovering: pause silently, look at your notes, then 'Where was I? Right, the costs.' / 'Let me go back a step.' / 'Let me put that another way.' (when the audience looks confused or you've said something badly).

Difficult questions: listen to the end (don't interrupt or start answering halfway), thank or acknowledge (Thank you, that's a fair point. / I understand your concern.), rephrase the question neutrally, which also removes the anger and gives you time (So your question is whether the budget is realistic.), answer briefly (one point and one reason or example), admit what you don't know and promise a specific follow-up (I don't have that figure with me, but I'll send it to you by Friday.), agree with the part that is true (You're right that the first month was difficult.), park off-topic questions (That's a bit outside today's topic, but I'm happy to discuss it after the session.) and bridge back to your message (That brings me back to my main point: …). Indonesian habits to name respectfully: avoiding 'I don't know' to save face (gengsi, malu) and bluffing instead; staying silent or apologising too much when a senior person challenges you; in English, calm and honest sounds professional. Keep 'I'm afraid' = sayangnya (recap).

Limits: A0–B2 grammar plus the chain. No cleft sentences ('What we need is …', 'It was Sari who …'), inversion or subjunctive in examples; 'What's interesting here is that …' is a phrase to remember from b2. Don't teach slide design, body language, sales psychology or debate techniques in depth. Many choices are style (several hooks can work; To sum up / In short are both fine): test only clear cases, such as a real hook versus a name-and-topic opening, a keyword note versus a full sentence, a calm reply versus a defensive or bluffing one. Listening items use one voice and no speaker labels. Correct one thing at a time.

keyPoints.title: Tell a story to persuade
keyPoints.explanation: Open with a hook (a question, a surprising number or a very short story), not only your name and topic. Tell a short story in four parts: the situation, the turning point, the change and the lesson for the audience, with concrete detail (a name, a place, a number). Use past tenses for the story and the present for the point. Give your reasons in threes, and end with a call to action: who does what by when.

examples.en: How many of you have waited more than an hour at a bank this year?
examples.id: Berapa banyak dari Anda yang pernah menunggu lebih dari satu jam di bank tahun ini?

examples.en: Last March, Pak Joko, a batik seller in Solo, was losing three orders a week because his parcels arrived late.
examples.id: Maret lalu, Pak Joko, penjual batik di Solo, kehilangan tiga pesanan setiap minggu karena paketnya datang terlambat.

examples.en: So please send me your branch's answer by the end of this month.
examples.id: Jadi, mohon kirimkan jawaban cabang Anda kepada saya paling lambat akhir bulan ini.

id.title: Bercerita untuk meyakinkan
id.explanation: Buka dengan hook (pengait): pertanyaan, angka yang mengejutkan atau cerita yang sangat singkat, bukan hanya nama dan topikmu. Ceritakan kisah pendek dalam empat bagian: situasinya, titik baliknya, perubahannya dan pelajaran untuk audiens, dengan detail konkret (nama, tempat, angka). Pakai bentuk lampau untuk ceritanya dan bentuk sekarang (present) untuk poinnya. Sampaikan alasanmu dalam kelompok tiga, dan tutup dengan call to action (ajakan bertindak): siapa melakukan apa, kapan.

keyPoints.title: Present from brief notes, not a script
keyPoints.explanation: Write keyword notes, not full sentences: a few words per idea, mostly names, numbers and key words. Reading a script sounds flat, because your eyes are on the paper and written sentences are long. Rehearse aloud from the keywords several times, and learn only your first and last lines by heart. Use slides as prompts: one idea per slide. If you lose your place, pause, look at your notes and say: Where was I? Right, …

examples.id: Catatan kata kunci untuk: pengiriman di Surabaya turun dari 5 menjadi 2 hari (setelah ada gudang baru).

examples.en: Where was I? Right, the costs.
examples.id: Tadi sampai mana, ya? Oh iya, biayanya.

examples.en: Let me go back a step.

id.title: Presentasi dengan catatan singkat, bukan naskah
id.explanation: Tulis catatan kata kunci, bukan kalimat lengkap: beberapa kata per ide, terutama nama, angka dan kata kunci. Membaca naskah terdengar datar, karena matamu tertuju ke kertas dan kalimat tulisan itu panjang. Berlatihlah dengan suara keras dari kata kunci itu beberapa kali, dan hafalkan hanya kalimat pertama dan terakhirmu. Pakai slide sebagai pengingat: satu ide per slide. Kalau kamu lupa sampai mana, berhenti sejenak, lihat catatanmu dan katakan: Where was I? Right, …

keyPoints.title: Handle difficult questions calmly
keyPoints.explanation: Listen to the end, then thank or acknowledge the person (Thank you, that's a fair point.). Rephrase the question calmly (So your question is whether …), answer briefly, and admit what you don't know with a clear follow-up (I don't have that figure with me, but I'll send it to you by Friday.). Agree with what is true, park off-topic questions politely, and bridge back to your main message. Don't argue, don't bluff.

examples.en: I understand your concern, and you're right that the first month was difficult.
examples.id: Saya memahami kekhawatiran Anda, dan Anda benar bahwa bulan pertama memang sulit.

examples.en: So your question is whether the app is worth the cost.
examples.id: Jadi pertanyaan Anda adalah apakah aplikasinya sepadan dengan biayanya.

examples.en: I don't have that figure with me, but I'll send it to you by Friday.
examples.id: Saya tidak membawa angka itu, tapi akan saya kirimkan kepada Anda paling lambat hari Jumat.

id.title: Menghadapi pertanyaan sulit dengan tenang
id.explanation: Dengarkan sampai selesai, lalu ucapkan terima kasih atau akui poin orang itu (Thank you, that's a fair point.). Ulangi pertanyaannya dengan kata-katamu sendiri secara tenang (So your question is whether …), jawab dengan singkat, dan akui apa yang tidak kamu ketahui dengan tindak lanjut yang jelas (I don't have that figure with me, but I'll send it to you by Friday.). Setujui bagian yang memang benar, tunda pertanyaan di luar topik dengan sopan, dan kembalikan pembicaraan ke pesan utamamu. Jangan berdebat, jangan pura-pura tahu.

guidedPractice.prompt: You've told your story about a customer in the past. Now give the point for the audience, in the present. Complete with the right form of show: This story ___ why fast replies matter.
guidedPractice.hint: The point is about now, and the subject is 'this story' (he/she/it): add -s.

guidedPractice.prompt: End your talk with a call to action. Complete with one word: Let's ___ a three-month pilot in Bandung in January.
You skipped a step in your explanation and want to return to it. Complete with one word: Let me go ___ a step.
Someone asks for a number you don't have. Be honest and promise a follow-up. Complete with one word: I don't have that figure with me, but I'll ___ it to you by Friday.
A manager says your timeline is too short. Acknowledge it calmly before you answer. Complete with one word: Thank you, that's a fair ___.
guidedPractice.hint: poin yang masuk akal = a fair …

independentPractice.prompt: Your colleague's slides are full of paragraphs. Give her the rule. Complete with one word: one ___ per slide.
You've answered a hostile question and want to return to your message. Complete with one word: That brings me ___ to my main point.
independentPractice.hint: membawa saya kembali ke … = brings me … to

independentPractice.prompt: You're telling a story about a customer. Keep it in the past. Complete with the right form of call: Last month, a restaurant owner in Medan ___ us at midnight because her order was missing.
independentPractice.hint: Indonesian doesn't change the verb (menelepon), but English needs the past: -ed.

assessment.prompt: Bu Ani opens her talk to the sales team in Bandung like this, before she says her name: 'Nine out of ten customers who complain to us never order again.' Which kind of hook is it? Choose from: a question, a surprising number, a short story. Write your choice.
assessment.rubric: Correct: a surprising number (nine out of ten is a striking figure that makes people want to hear more). 'a statistic' / 'a surprising fact' = 100 (same idea). 'a question' = 0 (it's a statement, not a question to the audience). 'a short story' = 10 (there's no person, place or event in time: no situation, turning point or change).

assessment.prompt: Rina has just told her story about Pak Joko, a batik seller in Solo whose parcels arrived late last year. Now she gives the point for her audience: what the company should do now. Complete with the right form of need: That's why our company ___ a second warehouse in Central Java.
assessment.rubric: Correct: needs (the story is in the past, but the point is about now: present simple, and our company = it, so -s). 'really / urgently / now needs' = 100. 'need' = 50 (right tense, but our company needs -s). 'needed' = 30 (past: it sounds like an old need, not what to do now). 'is needing' = 20 (need is a state verb: no -ing here). 'will need' = 60 (possible, but weaker than the present for a point about now).

assessment.prompt: Three sentences from Sari's story at an NGO meeting: (1) 'Two years ago, we started a reading programme in twenty schools in Lombok.' (2) 'Then, after three months, half of the children stopped coming.' (3) 'So we moved the classes to the afternoon, and attendance went up to ninety percent.' Which part of the story is sentence 2? Choose from: the situation, the turning point, the change, the lesson. Write your choice.
assessment.rubric: Correct: the turning point (the moment the problem became clear: half of the children stopped coming). 'the problem' = 100 (the turning point is the problem). 'the situation' = 20 (that's sentence 1: who, where, when). 'the change' = 10 (that's sentence 3: what they did and what happened). 'the lesson' = 0 (none of these sentences gives the point for the audience yet).

assessment.prompt: Sari wants to speak from notes, not read. One sentence in her script is: 'After three months, more than 500 farmers in Garut were using the app every week.' Write a keyword note for it of at most four words, with only the key facts.
assessment.rubric: A good note keeps the number (500) and who or where (farmers, Garut), in 2–4 words, with no full sentence: for example 'Garut: 500+ farmers' or '500 farmers / week'. Any order and symbols (+, :, /) are fine = 100. '500 farmers' alone = 90 (Garut is useful but the slide or context may show it). Keywords without the number (e.g. 'farmers Garut app') = 40 (the key fact is lost). More than four words but still notes = 60. A full sentence, or most of the script copied = 10 (that's a script, not a note).

assessment.prompt: Halfway through your talk at a university seminar in Bandung, you notice confused faces after a long, technical sentence. You want to say it again, more simply. Complete with one word: Let me put that another ___.
assessment.rubric: Correct: way (Let me put that another way = saya jelaskan dengan cara lain). 'ways' = 60 (another + singular). 'word' or 'words' = 40 ('Let me put that in other words' is a different phrase). 'time' = 10 (that would just repeat it).

assessment.prompt: In the Q&A at a ministry in Jakarta, a director says angrily: 'This budget is completely unrealistic!' You reply calmly: 'So your question is whether we can deliver the project with this budget.' Which move is your reply? Choose from: acknowledge, rephrase, admit, bridge back. Write your choice.
assessment.rubric: Correct: rephrase (you turn an angry statement into a calm, neutral question in your own words, which also gives you time). 'paraphrase' = 100. 'acknowledge' = 20 (that would be 'Thank you, that's a fair concern' or 'I understand your concern'). 'admit' = 0 (you aren't saying what you don't know). 'bridge back' = 10 (that returns to your main message after the answer).

assessment.prompt: At your seminar on online marketing for small shops in Yogyakarta, someone asks about the new tax rules for small businesses. That isn't your topic. Park the question politely. Complete with one word: That's a bit ___ today's topic, but I'm happy to discuss it after the session.
assessment.rubric: Correct: outside (a bit outside today's topic = agak di luar topik hari ini). 'beyond' and 'off' = 100. 'out of' = 50 (understood, but 'outside' is the natural word here). 'about' or 'from' = 10 (they don't say it's off topic). 'out' alone = 40.

material.title: Open with a hook, end with a call to action

blocks.text:
Quick recap: from the B2 presentations lesson you have the **signposts** (*Today I'd like to talk about …*, *Let's move on to …*, *To sum up, …*); from the prosody lesson, the **voice**: step up on the key word, pause before a key number, fall ↘ at the end of a point. Now the two moments people remember most: **the first 30 seconds and the last 30 seconds**.

**1. The hook.** A **hook** (kail, pengait) is an opening that makes people *want* to listen. Three reliable kinds:
- **A question to the audience:** ***How many of you have waited more than an hour at a bank this year?***
- **A surprising number:** ***Last year, one in four of our new customers left within a month.***
- **A very short story:** ***Last March, Bu Siti, a market trader in Surabaya, queued for two hours to send money to her son.***
Your name and topic still matter: give them **right after** the hook, briefly (*I'm Dimas from the IT team, and today I'd like to show you how we can fix that.*).

**2. The rule of three.** Give **three** reasons, benefits or steps. Three sounds complete and is easy to remember: ***It's faster, cheaper and safer.*** Let your voice fall ↘ on the last one.

**3. The call to action.** A **call to action** (ajakan bertindak) tells the audience **who does what by when**. It's the reason you're presenting, so make it the last thing they hear before *Thank you*:
- ***So I'm asking you to approve a three-month pilot in Bandung, starting in January.***
- ***Please send me your branch's answer by the end of this month.***
- ***Let's start with one city and measure the results.***
Not `That's all. Thank you.` ✗ or `Okay, that's it.` ✗: the audience leaves without knowing what you want from them.

id.text:
Ulasan singkat: dari pelajaran presentasi B2 kamu sudah punya **signpost** (*Today I'd like to talk about …*, *Let's move on to …*, *To sum up, …*); dari pelajaran prosodi, **suaranya**: naikkan nada di kata kunci, beri jeda sebelum angka penting, turunkan nada ↘ di akhir poin. Sekarang dua momen yang paling diingat orang: **30 detik pertama dan 30 detik terakhir**.

**1. Hook.** **Hook** (kail, pengait) adalah pembukaan yang membuat orang *ingin* mendengarkan. Tiga jenis yang bisa diandalkan:
- **Pertanyaan untuk audiens:** ***How many of you have waited more than an hour at a bank this year?*** (berapa banyak dari Anda yang pernah menunggu lebih dari satu jam di bank tahun ini?)
- **Angka yang mengejutkan:** ***Last year, one in four of our new customers left within a month.*** (tahun lalu, satu dari empat pelanggan baru kita pergi dalam sebulan)
- **Cerita yang sangat singkat:** ***Last March, Bu Siti, a market trader in Surabaya, queued for two hours to send money to her son.*** (Maret lalu, Bu Siti, pedagang pasar di Surabaya, antre dua jam untuk mengirim uang kepada anaknya)
Nama dan topikmu tetap penting: sebutkan **tepat setelah** hook, dengan singkat (*I'm Dimas from the IT team, and today I'd like to show you how we can fix that.*).

**2. Rule of three (aturan tiga).** Sampaikan **tiga** alasan, manfaat atau langkah. Tiga terdengar lengkap dan mudah diingat: ***It's faster, cheaper and safer.*** (lebih cepat, lebih murah dan lebih aman) Turunkan nada ↘ di yang terakhir.

**3. Call to action.** **Call to action** (ajakan bertindak) memberi tahu audiens **siapa melakukan apa, kapan**. Inilah alasan kamu presentasi, jadi jadikan itu hal terakhir yang mereka dengar sebelum *Thank you*:
- ***So I'm asking you to approve a three-month pilot in Bandung, starting in January.*** (jadi saya meminta Anda menyetujui uji coba tiga bulan di Bandung, mulai Januari)
- ***Please send me your branch's answer by the end of this month.*** (mohon kirimkan jawaban cabang Anda paling lambat akhir bulan ini)
- ***Let's start with one city and measure the results.*** (mari kita mulai dari satu kota dan ukur hasilnya)
Bukan `That's all. Thank you.` ✗ atau `Okay, that's it.` ✗: audiens pulang tanpa tahu apa yang kamu inginkan dari mereka.

id.note: call to action: siapa (Anda), apa (kirim jawaban), kapan

blocks.text:
Indonesian habits, named with respect:
- **The long thank-you opening.** *Pertama-tama, puji syukur …, terima kasih kepada Bapak Direktur, Bapak/Ibu manajer, panitia …* is warm and polite in Indonesian. In English, a minute of thanks uses up the 30 seconds when people listen best. One short thank-you is enough (*Thank you for having me.*), and it can come after the hook.
- **Only name and topic.** `Good morning. My name is Dimas, and today I will talk about our mobile app.` isn't wrong, but it gives nobody a reason to listen. Put a hook first.
- **The ending that just stops.** `That's all. Thank you.` ✗ → call to action, then ***Thank you.***

id.text:
Kebiasaan kita, disebut dengan hormat:
- **Pembukaan terima kasih yang panjang.** *Pertama-tama, puji syukur …, terima kasih kepada Bapak Direktur, Bapak/Ibu manajer, panitia …* itu hangat dan sopan dalam bahasa Indonesia. Dalam bahasa Inggris, satu menit ucapan terima kasih menghabiskan 30 detik saat orang paling mau mendengarkan. Satu ucapan terima kasih singkat sudah cukup (*Thank you for having me.*), dan boleh diucapkan setelah hook.
- **Hanya nama dan topik.** `Good morning. My name is Dimas, and today I will talk about our mobile app.` tidak salah, tapi tidak memberi alasan bagi siapa pun untuk mendengarkan. Taruh hook di depan.
- **Penutup yang tiba-tiba berhenti.** `That's all. Thank you.` ✗ → call to action, lalu ***Thank you.***

blocks.prompt: Bu Ani is ending her talk to branch managers about a new training programme. Which ending is a clear call to action?
options: Okay, that's all from me. Thank you.
So please choose two people from your branch and send me their names by Friday. Thank you.
I hope this presentation was useful for all of you. Thank you very much.
blocks.explain: It says **who** (you, the branch managers), **what** (choose two people, send their names) and **when** (by Friday). The first one just stops, and the third one is polite but asks for nothing: the managers leave without knowing what to do.

id.prompt: Bu Ani menutup presentasinya untuk para manajer cabang tentang program pelatihan baru. Penutup mana yang merupakan call to action yang jelas?
id.explain: Penutup ini menyebutkan **siapa** (Anda, para manajer cabang), **apa** (pilih dua orang, kirim nama mereka) dan **kapan** (paling lambat Jumat). Yang pertama tiba-tiba berhenti, dan yang ketiga sopan tapi tidak meminta apa-apa: para manajer pulang tanpa tahu apa yang harus dilakukan.

id.title: Buka dengan hook, tutup dengan call to action

material.title: A short story with a point

blocks.text:
Numbers convince the head; a story makes people **care**. In a presentation, a good story is short (30–60 seconds) and has **four parts**:
1. **The situation:** who, where, when. *Last year, Pak Joko, a batik seller in Solo, was sending about forty parcels a week through us.*
2. **The turning point:** the moment the problem became clear. *Then, one Monday in March, his biggest customer cancelled an order worth twenty million rupiah, because it was late again.*
3. **The change:** what was done, and what happened. *We moved his parcels to our new warehouse in Semarang, and his late deliveries fell to zero.*
4. **The lesson for the audience:** the point, linked to what you want. *That's why I believe we need a second warehouse in Central Java.*

**Concrete detail** makes a story believable: **a name, a place, a number**. *Pak Joko, a batik seller in Solo, lost three orders a week* is much stronger than *many customers have problems*.

**Tenses:** tell the story in the **past** (past simple for the events: *called, cancelled, moved*; past continuous for the background: *was sending, was losing*), then switch to the **present** for the point, because the point is about **now**: *That's why I **believe** we **need** …*

Why might you hear a native speaker say *So last week this customer **calls** me …*? In relaxed, informal storytelling, some people use the present to make a story feel live. It's a style choice, not a mistake. In a presentation, the past is the safe choice; just don't jump between the two at random.

id.text:
Angka meyakinkan kepala; cerita membuat orang **peduli**. Dalam presentasi, cerita yang baik itu singkat (30–60 detik) dan punya **empat bagian**:
1. **Situasinya:** siapa, di mana, kapan. *Last year, Pak Joko, a batik seller in Solo, was sending about forty parcels a week through us.* (tahun lalu, Pak Joko, penjual batik di Solo, mengirim sekitar empat puluh paket seminggu lewat kami)
2. **Titik baliknya (turning point):** saat masalahnya menjadi jelas. *Then, one Monday in March, his biggest customer cancelled an order worth twenty million rupiah, because it was late again.* (lalu, suatu Senin di bulan Maret, pelanggan terbesarnya membatalkan pesanan senilai dua puluh juta rupiah, karena terlambat lagi)
3. **Perubahannya:** apa yang dilakukan, dan apa yang terjadi. *We moved his parcels to our new warehouse in Semarang, and his late deliveries fell to zero.* (kami memindahkan paketnya ke gudang baru kami di Semarang, dan keterlambatannya turun menjadi nol)
4. **Pelajaran untuk audiens:** poinnya, dihubungkan dengan apa yang kamu inginkan. *That's why I believe we need a second warehouse in Central Java.* (karena itulah saya yakin kita butuh gudang kedua di Jawa Tengah)

**Detail konkret** membuat cerita bisa dipercaya: **nama, tempat, angka**. *Pak Joko, a batik seller in Solo, lost three orders a week* jauh lebih kuat daripada *many customers have problems* (banyak pelanggan punya masalah).

**Tenses (bentuk waktu):** ceritakan kisahnya dalam bentuk **lampau** (past simple untuk kejadiannya: *called, cancelled, moved*; past continuous untuk latarnya: *was sending, was losing*), lalu pindah ke bentuk **sekarang** (present) untuk poinnya, karena poinnya tentang **saat ini**: *That's why I **believe** we **need** …*

Kenapa kadang kamu mendengar penutur asli bilang *So last week this customer **calls** me …*? Saat bercerita santai, sebagian orang memakai bentuk sekarang supaya ceritanya terasa hidup. Itu pilihan gaya, bukan kesalahan. Dalam presentasi, bentuk lampau adalah pilihan yang aman; yang penting jangan berpindah-pindah di antara keduanya secara acak.

rows.en: Two years ago, Dr. Wulan was running a small clinic in Yogyakarta with three nurses.
rows.id: Dua tahun lalu, Dr. Wulan mengelola klinik kecil di Yogyakarta dengan tiga perawat.
rows.note: situation: past continuous for the background

rows.en: One morning, forty patients were waiting outside before the clinic even opened.
rows.id: Suatu pagi, empat puluh pasien sudah menunggu di luar bahkan sebelum klinik buka.
rows.note: turning point: the problem becomes clear

rows.en: She started online bookings, and the queue disappeared within a month.
rows.id: Dia memulai pendaftaran online, dan antreannya hilang dalam sebulan.
rows.note: the change: past simple for the events

rows.en: Small clinics don't need big budgets. They need simple tools.
rows.id: Klinik kecil tidak butuh anggaran besar. Mereka butuh alat yang sederhana.
rows.note: the lesson: present, because it's true now

blocks.text:
Indonesian traps in stories:
- **No past ending.** Indonesian doesn't change the verb for the past (*bulan lalu pelanggan menelepon kami*), so the ending disappears: `Last month a customer call us` ✗ → ***Last month a customer called us.*** In a story, listen to yourself for **-ed** and irregular pasts (*lost, sent, came*).
- **A story with no point.** A nice story that ends with *… and that's what happened* leaves the audience asking *so what?* Always add the lesson: ***That's why …*** / ***So the lesson for us is simple: …***
- **Too general.** *Many customers have problems with delivery* → give one real (or clearly practice) customer with a name, a place and a number.

id.text:
Jebakan dalam bercerita:
- **Tanpa akhiran lampau.** Bahasa Indonesia tidak mengubah kata kerja untuk masa lampau (*bulan lalu pelanggan menelepon kami*), jadi akhirannya hilang: `Last month a customer call us` ✗ → ***Last month a customer called us.*** Saat bercerita, perhatikan **-ed** dan bentuk lampau tak beraturan (*lost, sent, came*).
- **Cerita tanpa poin.** Cerita yang menarik tapi diakhiri dengan *… and that's what happened* membuat audiens bertanya *lalu kenapa?* Selalu tambahkan pelajarannya: ***That's why …*** (karena itulah …) / ***So the lesson for us is simple: …*** (jadi pelajarannya bagi kita sederhana: …)
- **Terlalu umum.** *Many customers have problems with delivery* → berikan satu pelanggan nyata (atau jelas-jelas contoh latihan) dengan nama, tempat dan angka.

blocks.prompt: Which sentence would be the best lesson for the audience at the end of Dr. Wulan's story?
options: She started online bookings in May.
Small clinics don't need big budgets: they need simple tools, and we can give them those tools this year.
And that was the story of Dr. Wulan's clinic.
blocks.explain: The lesson turns the story into a point for **this** audience, in the **present**, and links it to what you want (*we can give them those tools this year*). The first one is still part of the story (the change), and the third one ends without a point.

id.prompt: Kalimat mana yang paling baik sebagai pelajaran untuk audiens di akhir cerita Dr. Wulan?
id.explain: Pelajarannya mengubah cerita menjadi poin untuk audiens **ini**, dalam bentuk **sekarang** (present), dan menghubungkannya dengan apa yang kamu inginkan (*we can give them those tools this year*). Yang pertama masih bagian dari ceritanya (perubahannya), dan yang ketiga berakhir tanpa poin.

material.title: Speak from notes, not a script

blocks.text:
**Why reading sounds flat.** When you read a script, your eyes are on the paper, so there's no eye contact. Written sentences are long, so you pause where the line ends, not where the idea ends, and your voice loses the pitch range you practised in the prosody lesson. The audience hears a voice reading, not a person talking to them.

**Keyword notes** (catatan kata kunci) are a few words per idea, mostly **names, numbers and key words**, with arrows and symbols. Never full sentences.
- Script: *Our delivery time in Surabaya fell from five days to two after we opened the new warehouse.*
- Note: **Surabaya delivery: 5 → 2 days (new warehouse)**
You make the sentence again, live, each time. That's why you sound natural.

**A rehearsal method:**
1. Write a full draft once, to find your ideas.
2. Cut it down to keyword notes.
3. Say the talk **aloud** from the notes three or four times. Different words each time is fine.
4. Time it, and record yourself or practise with a colleague.
5. Learn by heart **only** your first and last lines: the hook and the call to action.

**Slides as prompts.** Put **one idea per slide**: a short headline and one number or picture. The slide reminds *you* what to say, and the audience listens to you instead of reading.

**If you lose your place:** stop, stay silent for a second (silence, not *eee…*), look at your notes, then:
- ***Where was I? Right, the costs.***
- ***Let me go back a step.***
- ***Let me put that another way.*** (when you said it badly or people look confused)

id.text:
**Kenapa membaca terdengar datar.** Saat membaca naskah, matamu tertuju ke kertas, jadi tidak ada kontak mata. Kalimat tulisan itu panjang, jadi kamu berhenti di tempat barisnya habis, bukan di tempat idenya selesai, dan suaramu kehilangan rentang nada yang sudah kamu latih di pelajaran prosodi. Audiens mendengar suara yang sedang membaca, bukan orang yang berbicara kepada mereka.

**Catatan kata kunci** (keyword notes) adalah beberapa kata per ide, terutama **nama, angka dan kata kunci**, dengan panah dan simbol. Jangan pernah kalimat lengkap.
- Naskah: *Our delivery time in Surabaya fell from five days to two after we opened the new warehouse.* (waktu pengiriman kami di Surabaya turun dari lima hari menjadi dua setelah kami membuka gudang baru)
- Catatan: **Surabaya delivery: 5 → 2 days (new warehouse)**
Kamu menyusun kalimatnya lagi, secara langsung, setiap kali. Itulah sebabnya kamu terdengar alami.

**Cara berlatih:**
1. Tulis draf lengkap satu kali, untuk menemukan ide-idemu.
2. Ringkas menjadi catatan kata kunci.
3. Bawakan presentasinya **dengan suara keras** dari catatan itu tiga atau empat kali. Kata-katanya berbeda setiap kali juga tidak apa-apa.
4. Ukur waktunya, dan rekam dirimu atau berlatih dengan rekan kerja.
5. Hafalkan **hanya** kalimat pertama dan terakhirmu: hook dan call to action.

**Slide sebagai pengingat.** Taruh **satu ide per slide**: judul singkat dan satu angka atau gambar. Slide itu mengingatkan *kamu* apa yang harus dikatakan, dan audiens mendengarkanmu, bukan membaca.

**Kalau kamu lupa sampai mana:** berhenti, diam sedetik (diam, bukan *eee…*), lihat catatanmu, lalu:
- ***Where was I? Right, the costs.*** (tadi sampai mana, ya? Oh iya, biayanya)
- ***Let me go back a step.*** (saya mundur selangkah dulu)
- ***Let me put that another way.*** (saya jelaskan dengan cara lain; saat kamu menyampaikannya kurang baik atau orang terlihat bingung)

rows.en: Most of our new users in Medan found the app through their friends, not through our ads.
rows.id: Kebanyakan pengguna baru kami di Medan menemukan aplikasinya lewat teman, bukan lewat iklan kami.

rows.en: The training cost us forty million rupiah, but it saved us twice that in the first year.
rows.id: Pelatihannya menghabiskan empat puluh juta rupiah, tapi menghemat dua kali lipatnya di tahun pertama.

rows.en: Where was I? Right, the costs.
rows.id: Tadi sampai mana, ya? Oh iya, biayanya.
rows.note: after a silent pause and a look at your notes

id.note: setelah jeda tanpa suara dan melihat catatan

rows.en: Let me go back a step.

blocks.text:
Two habits from school that don't help here:
- **Reading the slides** (recap from B2): if the slide has a paragraph, people read it faster than you speak and stop listening. One idea per slide.
- **Hafalan, learning the script word for word.** It feels safe, but if you forget one word, everything stops, and you sound like you're reciting. Learn the **ideas** and their order; learn by heart only the first and last lines.
And if you lose your place, don't apologise again and again (`Sorry, sorry, I forgot… eee… apa ya…` ✗). A calm pause and ***Where was I?*** look confident: everybody loses their place sometimes.

id.text:
Dua kebiasaan dari sekolah yang tidak membantu di sini:
- **Membaca slide** (ulasan dari B2): kalau slide berisi satu paragraf, orang membacanya lebih cepat daripada kamu bicara dan berhenti mendengarkan. Satu ide per slide.
- **Hafalan, menghafal naskah kata per kata.** Terasa aman, tapi kalau kamu lupa satu kata, semuanya berhenti, dan kamu terdengar seperti sedang membaca hafalan. Hafalkan **ide-idenya** dan urutannya; hafalkan kata per kata hanya kalimat pertama dan terakhir.
Dan kalau kamu lupa sampai mana, jangan minta maaf berkali-kali (`Sorry, sorry, I forgot… eee… apa ya…` ✗). Jeda yang tenang dan ***Where was I?*** terlihat percaya diri: semua orang kadang lupa sampai mana.

blocks.prompt: Dimas is preparing a ten-minute talk for investors in Jakarta. Which plan is best?
options: Write the full script, put it on the slides, and read it carefully so he makes no mistakes.
Learn the whole script by heart, word for word, the night before.
Make keyword notes, rehearse aloud from them a few times, and learn only his first and last lines by heart.
blocks.explain: Keyword notes let him build the sentences live, so he sounds like a person talking, not reading. Rehearsing aloud makes the ideas and their order stick. Reading the slides loses the audience, and a word-for-word memorised script breaks down as soon as he forgets one word.

id.prompt: Dimas sedang menyiapkan presentasi sepuluh menit untuk para investor di Jakarta. Rencana mana yang terbaik?
id.explain: Catatan kata kunci membuatnya menyusun kalimat secara langsung, jadi dia terdengar seperti orang yang berbicara, bukan membaca. Berlatih dengan suara keras membuat ide dan urutannya melekat. Membaca slide membuat audiens tidak mendengarkan, dan naskah yang dihafal kata per kata langsung buyar begitu dia lupa satu kata.
options: Tulis naskah lengkap di slide dan baca dengan teliti agar tidak salah.
Hafalkan seluruh naskah kata demi kata pada malam sebelumnya.
Buat catatan kata kunci, latihan bersuara beberapa kali, dan hafalkan hanya pembuka serta penutupnya.

blocks.text:
Recap from B2: welcome the question, check it, answer briefly, then *Does that answer your question?* Now the hard ones: the hostile question, the one you can't answer, and the off-topic one.

1. **Listen to the end.** Don't interrupt, and don't start answering halfway. You'll often find the real question in the last sentence.
2. **Thank or acknowledge.** ***Thank you, that's a fair point.*** / ***I understand your concern.*** Acknowledging the feeling isn't agreeing with everything.
3. **Rephrase the question** in calm, neutral words: ***So your question is whether the budget is realistic.*** This takes the anger out, checks that you understood, and gives you a few seconds to think.
4. **Answer briefly:** one point and one reason or example. Agree with the part that is true: ***You're right that the first month was difficult. Since then, …***
5. **Admit what you don't know**, with a specific follow-up: ***I don't have that figure with me, but I'll send it to you by Friday.***
6. **Off-topic?** Park it politely: ***That's a bit outside today's topic, but I'm happy to discuss it after the session.***
7. **Bridge back** to your message: ***That brings me back to my main point: …***

Never: `That's not true. You don't understand.` ✗ (defensive), `No comment.` ✗ (sounds like hiding something), or a guessed number.

id.text:
Ulasan dari B2: sambut pertanyaannya, cek, jawab singkat, lalu *Does that answer your question?* Sekarang yang sulit: pertanyaan yang bernada menyerang (hostile), pertanyaan yang tidak bisa kamu jawab, dan pertanyaan di luar topik.

1. **Dengarkan sampai selesai.** Jangan memotong, dan jangan mulai menjawab di tengah. Pertanyaan yang sebenarnya sering ada di kalimat terakhir.
2. **Ucapkan terima kasih atau akui poinnya.** ***Thank you, that's a fair point.*** (terima kasih, itu poin yang masuk akal) / ***I understand your concern.*** (saya memahami kekhawatiran Anda) Mengakui perasaan orang tidak sama dengan menyetujui semuanya.
3. **Ulangi pertanyaannya dengan kata-katamu sendiri** (rephrase), dengan kata-kata yang tenang dan netral: ***So your question is whether the budget is realistic.*** (jadi pertanyaan Anda adalah apakah anggarannya realistis) Ini meredakan emosinya, memastikan kamu paham, dan memberimu beberapa detik untuk berpikir.
4. **Jawab singkat:** satu poin dan satu alasan atau contoh. Setujui bagian yang memang benar: ***You're right that the first month was difficult. Since then, …*** (Anda benar bahwa bulan pertama memang sulit. Sejak itu, …)
5. **Akui apa yang tidak kamu ketahui**, dengan tindak lanjut yang spesifik: ***I don't have that figure with me, but I'll send it to you by Friday.*** (saya tidak membawa angka itu, tapi akan saya kirimkan paling lambat hari Jumat)
6. **Di luar topik?** Tunda dengan sopan: ***That's a bit outside today's topic, but I'm happy to discuss it after the session.*** (itu agak di luar topik hari ini, tapi dengan senang hati saya bahas setelah sesi ini)
7. **Kembali (bridge back)** ke pesanmu: ***That brings me back to my main point: …*** (itu membawa saya kembali ke poin utama saya: …)

Jangan pernah: `That's not true. You don't understand.` ✗ (defensif), `No comment.` ✗ (terdengar seperti menyembunyikan sesuatu), atau angka tebakan.

rows.en: Thank you, Pak Hasan. I understand your concern about the timeline.
rows.id: Terima kasih, Pak Hasan. Saya memahami kekhawatiran Anda soal jadwalnya.

rows.en: So your question is whether we can finish the project by June.
rows.id: Jadi pertanyaan Anda adalah apakah kita bisa menyelesaikan proyeknya paling lambat Juni.

id.note: mengulang dengan kata sendiri: tenang dan netral

rows.en: You're right that the first month was difficult. Since then, complaints have fallen by half.
rows.id: Anda benar bahwa bulan pertama memang sulit. Sejak itu, keluhan sudah turun setengahnya.
rows.note: agree with what is true, then answer

rows.en: I'm afraid I don't know the cost for each province yet, but I'll check and email you tomorrow.
rows.id: Sayangnya saya belum tahu biaya untuk setiap provinsi, tapi akan saya cek dan saya email besok.

rows.en: That brings me back to my main point: we need to start small.
rows.id: Itu membawa saya kembali ke poin utama saya: kita perlu mulai dari skala kecil.

blocks.text:
Two Indonesian traps:
- **Avoiding *I don't know*.** Not knowing in front of a director can feel like losing face (gengsi, malu), so some presenters guess, or answer a different question. In English, an honest ***I don't have that figure with me, but I'll send it to you by Friday*** sounds professional, as long as you really send it by Friday. A guess that turns out wrong costs you much more.
- **Going silent or apologising when a senior person challenges you.** Being respectful doesn't mean giving up your point. Thank them, rephrase calmly, and answer: ***Thank you, Bu Ani. You're right that the costs are high. Here's why we think they're worth it.***

id.text:
Dua jebakan untuk kita:
- **Menghindari *I don't know*.** Tidak tahu di depan direktur bisa terasa seperti kehilangan muka (gengsi, malu), jadi sebagian presenter menebak, atau menjawab pertanyaan yang lain. Dalam bahasa Inggris, ***I don't have that figure with me, but I'll send it to you by Friday*** yang jujur terdengar profesional, asalkan kamu benar-benar mengirimnya paling lambat Jumat. Tebakan yang ternyata salah jauh lebih merugikan.
- **Diam atau terus minta maaf saat orang yang lebih senior menyanggah.** Bersikap hormat tidak berarti melepaskan poinmu. Ucapkan terima kasih, ulangi pertanyaannya dengan tenang, lalu jawab: ***Thank you, Bu Ani. You're right that the costs are high. Here's why we think they're worth it.*** (terima kasih, Bu Ani. Anda benar bahwa biayanya tinggi. Ini alasan kami menganggapnya sepadan)

blocks.prompt: At a seminar in Bandung about your new delivery service, someone asks about the government's fuel prices next year. It isn't your topic. What's the best reply?
options: That's not my topic. Next question, please.
Fuel prices will probably go up by about ten percent, I think.
That's a bit outside today's topic, but I'm happy to talk about it after the session.
blocks.explain: It parks the question politely and offers a time to talk, so the person doesn't feel ignored. The first reply is true but sounds rude, and the second one is a guess about something you don't know.

id.prompt: Di sebuah seminar di Bandung tentang layanan pengiriman barumu, seseorang bertanya tentang harga BBM dari pemerintah tahun depan. Itu bukan topikmu. Jawaban mana yang terbaik?
id.explain: Jawaban ini menunda pertanyaannya dengan sopan dan menawarkan waktu untuk membahasnya, jadi orang itu tidak merasa diabaikan. Jawaban pertama benar tapi terdengar kasar, dan yang kedua adalah tebakan tentang sesuatu yang tidak kamu ketahui.

suggestedQuestions: Isn't it rude to start without thanking everyone first?
Can I tell a story about myself, or should it be about a customer?
How short should my keyword notes be?
What do I say when someone in the audience is openly angry with me?

flashcards.front: Berapa banyak dari Anda yang pernah …?
Karena itulah saya yakin kita butuh …
flashcards.back: That's why I believe we need …

Tadi sampai mana, ya? Oh iya, …

flashcards.back: Let me put that another way.

flashcards.back: Thank you, that's a fair point.

resources.title: Nancy Duarte uncovers common structure of greatest communicators
resources.note: A talk for native speakers on how persuasive talks move between 'what is' and 'what could be' and end with a call to action. Natural speed: watch with English subtitles if you need them, and notice the stories she uses.

id.note: Presentasi untuk penutur asli tentang bagaimana presentasi yang meyakinkan bergerak antara 'kondisi sekarang' dan 'kondisi yang bisa dicapai', lalu ditutup dengan ajakan bertindak. Kecepatan bicara alami: tonton dengan subtitle bahasa Inggris kalau perlu, dan perhatikan cerita-cerita yang dia pakai.

resources.title: Think Fast, Talk Smart: Communication Techniques
resources.source: Stanford Graduate School of Business (Matt Abrahams)
resources.note: A long lecture for native speakers on speaking without a script: managing nerves, answering questions you didn't expect and giving short, structured answers. Above the lesson's scope in places, but very practical for Q&A.

id.note: Kuliah panjang untuk penutur asli tentang berbicara tanpa naskah: mengelola rasa gugup, menjawab pertanyaan yang tidak terduga dan memberi jawaban yang singkat dan terstruktur. Di beberapa bagian melampaui cakupan pelajaran ini, tapi sangat praktis untuk sesi tanya jawab.

id.intro: Kamu sudah bisa memberi signpost dalam presentasi, menjelaskan grafik dan menjawab pertanyaan dengan jujur, dan kamu tahu cara membuat kata kuncimu menonjol lewat nada dan jeda. Sekarang kamu membuat presentasi yang **meyakinkan**: membuka dengan hook (pengait), menceritakan kisah pendek yang punya poin, menutup dengan ajakan bertindak yang jelas, berbicara dari catatan singkat alih-alih naskah, dan tetap tenang saat pertanyaannya sulit. Pemanasan: ingat satu presentasi yang benar-benar meyakinkanmu. Apa yang masih kamu ingat darinya?
suggestedQuestions: Apakah tidak sopan kalau aku langsung mulai tanpa berterima kasih kepada semua orang dulu?
Boleh aku bercerita tentang diriku sendiri, atau sebaiknya tentang pelanggan?
Seberapa singkat catatan kata kunciku sebaiknya?
Apa yang harus aku katakan kalau ada audiens yang terang-terangan marah kepadaku?

assessment.spa-1: Bu Ani membuka presentasinya untuk tim penjualan di Bandung seperti ini, sebelum menyebutkan namanya: 'Nine out of ten customers who complain to us never order again.' Hook jenis apa ini? Pilih dari: a question, a surprising number, a short story. Tulis pilihanmu.
assessment.spa-2: Rina baru saja menceritakan kisah Pak Joko, penjual batik di Solo yang paketnya datang terlambat tahun lalu. Sekarang dia menyampaikan poinnya untuk audiens: apa yang perlu dilakukan perusahaan sekarang. Lengkapi dengan bentuk yang tepat dari need: That's why our company ___ a second warehouse in Central Java.
assessment.spa-3: Tiga kalimat dari cerita Sari di rapat sebuah LSM: (1) 'Two years ago, we started a reading programme in twenty schools in Lombok.' (2) 'Then, after three months, half of the children stopped coming.' (3) 'So we moved the classes to the afternoon, and attendance went up to ninety percent.' Kalimat 2 termasuk bagian cerita yang mana? Pilih dari: the situation, the turning point, the change, the lesson. Tulis pilihanmu.
assessment.spa-4: Sari ingin berbicara dari catatan, bukan membaca. Salah satu kalimat di naskahnya: 'After three months, more than 500 farmers in Garut were using the app every week.' Tulis catatan kata kunci untuk kalimat itu dalam bahasa Inggris, paling banyak empat kata, berisi fakta utamanya saja.
assessment.spa-5: Di tengah presentasimu di seminar sebuah universitas di Bandung, kamu melihat wajah-wajah bingung setelah kalimat yang panjang dan teknis. Kamu ingin mengatakannya lagi dengan lebih sederhana. Lengkapi dengan satu kata: Let me put that another ___.
assessment.spa-6: Di sesi tanya jawab di sebuah kementerian di Jakarta, seorang direktur berkata dengan marah: 'This budget is completely unrealistic!' Kamu menjawab dengan tenang: 'So your question is whether we can deliver the project with this budget.' Langkah apa yang kamu lakukan? Pilih dari: acknowledge, rephrase, admit, bridge back. Tulis pilihanmu.
assessment.spa-7: Di seminarmu tentang pemasaran online untuk toko kecil di Yogyakarta, seseorang bertanya tentang aturan pajak baru untuk usaha kecil. Itu bukan topikmu. Tunda pertanyaannya dengan sopan. Lengkapi dengan satu kata: That's a bit ___ today's topic, but I'm happy to discuss it after the session.
